questions.q: Which cost component is often the single largest, despite never appearing on a provider's pricing page?
options: Data collection and labeling
Training compute
API authentication
Model versioning
questions.explain: Collecting, writing, and reviewing hundreds of good labeled examples is a human-hours cost that dwarfs training compute for most projects.

questions.q: What does OpenAI's fine-tuning job billing key off of, specifically?
options: The number of API calls made during training
trained_tokens — the total tokens the training run actually consumed
The number of employees on the account
A flat monthly subscription fee
questions.explain: trained_tokens (data size × epochs) is what training compute is billed on, as documented in the fine-tuning job object.

questions.q: What is true about inference cost for a typical fine-tuned model compared to its base model?
options: It is usually identical to the base model's rate
It is usually cheaper, since the model is more specialized
It is usually more expensive per call than the base model — a surcharge, not a discount
Fine-tuned models cannot be queried at inference time at all
questions.explain: Fine-tuned inference commonly carries a per-token surcharge over the base model's rate — a cost that compounds with call volume.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe fine-tuning as a recurring cost rather than a one-time cost?
options: Because API keys must be renewed every month
Because every fine-tuned model must be retrained daily regardless of circumstances
Because a fine-tune must be retrained whenever its underlying base model is deprecated
Because training data must be purchased fresh for every single API call
questions.explain: A fine-tune is tied to a specific base model version; when that base model is deprecated (Lesson 12), continuing to use the fine-tune means retraining on the new base model.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how should specific fine-tuning pricing figures (like dollars per million training tokens) be treated?
options: As fixed, permanent numbers that never need rechecking
As approximate and worth re-confirming against current provider pricing before budgeting
As irrelevant, since training is always free
As the single most important cost to track, more important than data collection
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly hedges specific pricing figures as approximate, since rates move and third-party figures can go stale quickly.
